title: I Built a Quantum Circuit That Mimics Classical Logic Gates — And You Won’t Believe What Happened!
bodyHtml:
I Built a Quantum Circuit That Mimics Classical Logic Gates — You Won’t Believe What Happened!

In our last blog, we peeled back the layers of quantum and classical hardware, revealing how ancient ideas have inspired today’s cutting-edge technology. But theory alone can only take you so far. For those who missed it, we dove into the physical foundations of classical and quantum systems and explored their fascinating differences. This time, I decided to take things further — why explain when I can show? So, I challenged myself to program a quantum circuit to replicate classical logic gates. Let’s dive in!

Quantum NOT:

This is one of the simplest implementation as the quantum single-qubit X/NOT gate acts similar to the classical NOT gate. This can be confirmed by verifying the truth table of classical NOT which is 0 turn to 1 and 1 turns to 0. This can be checked by calculating the result of the 0 ket applied X gate and the 1 ket (which can be simulated by adding one more X gate) to the circuit which will give 0 as a result, proving this circuit simulates classical NOT gate.

Quantum AND:

This gate is the tricky one, where instead of using 2 bits, we make use of 3 qubits using one (q[2]) of them just for measurement. The CCNOT gate returns NOT only when both inputs are 1 which is the same as classical AND logic. We can always verify this by cross-checking with the truth table of the classical version and adding X gates to the qubits used when we want the value 1.

Quantum NAND:

This shouldn’t be very difficult to deduce as NAND is simply AND + NOT and hence we arrangement the circuit using the same logical principle of negating the AND.

Quantum OR:

Because every classical gate can be ultimately broken down into a series of AND and NOT logics (in the real world, NAND gates, which are nothing but AND and NOT, are the heart of logic circuits in the modern machines) the OR gate can be defined as the NAND with NOT as both inputs, we did the same here. Look carefully to see the individual AND and NOT logic implementations in quantum.

Quantum NOR:

This again isn’t much of a surprise as we simply removed the NOT implementation from the previous circuit to give us NOR logic which is NOT of OR.

Quantum XOR:

Unlike NAND, NOR, and OR, and similar to AND and NOT this logic is uniquely defined though my previous statement remains true meaning even XOR can be broken down into a combination of NOTs and ANDs, though it can be messy and this is the simplest most optimized solution. So, a CNOT quantum gate doesn’t follow the same logic as a XOR, but gives the measurement like the XOR logic.

Still, note that unlike AND which requires an additional qubit to take in the measurement, CNOT-XOR implementation uses the same qubit for calculation as well as measurement. (Fun Fact: This gate is also responsible for the quantum phenomenon ENTANGLEMENT!)

Quantum 1-Bit Sub Adder:

This was a fun project I tried which adds qubit q[0] and q[1] and results in the sum c2[0] and carry c2[1] (measurements of q[1] and q[2]). To understand more about the Adder logic in classical logic gates, checkout the GeekForGeeks blog. The classical adder logic of sum is using the XOR gate which you can see in the quantum implementation as well as the AND implementation which is the logic for the carry bit. This 1-bit calculation provided me with the foundation to link multiple qubits to make the full adder circuit.

Quantum 2-bit Full Adder:

This was my final abstraction as bigger adders resulted in very complex and lengthy circuits which were just reappearance of this same circuit. Here we calculate the addition of q[1] q[0] + q[3] q[2] in respective place value system. So, a 1 in q[1] or q[3] means 2¹=2 whereas 1 in q[0] or q[2] means 2⁰=1.

I made the circuit using the same basic sub adder circuit but the important part was that the carry bit from the 2⁰ place value addition (q[0] + q[2]) and the sum bit of the 2¹ place value addition (q[1] + q[3]) will also need to be added to give the final carry bit. Here, the circuit might look incomplete but the final carry of the 2⁰ place addition (q[1] +q[3]) and the final carry bit also need to be added but it won’t result in a carry which is why we use only XOR/CNOT gate which is the sum logic.

I understand that this might be complex to understand and I haven’t explained it clearly although, the complete explanation will be too elaborate and there is a high chance of you loosing interest or getting demotivated when the logic actually is quite simple. Please try to decode this circuit on your own using a trace table recording the inputs and resultant outputs, and I’m sure it will be easier to understand.

As promised, I delivered the classical logic gate implementation using quantum gates. Here’s what I learned from this journey — and why it might just change how you think about quantum computing forever:

When I set out to program quantum circuits to mimic classical logic gates, I hit a wall with the AND gate. Unlike the simple 2-bit operation we’re familiar with in classical computing, the quantum equivalent required four registers — three quantum and one classical. This stark inefficiency highlights one of quantum computing’s biggest limitations: it’s not designed to mimic classical systems efficiently. Meanwhile, classical gates, when combined in intricate ways, have no trouble simulating quantum logic. In fact, the very backend simulators we use in Qiskit are powered by classical gates working tirelessly behind the scenes!

But here’s where things get interesting. This inefficiency turned out to be the key to solving the quantum adder exercise. Why? Because of the No-Cloning Theorem, a fundamental rule in quantum mechanics that states you cannot duplicate a quantum state. While it seems like a limitation, this unique property opened the door for us to evaluate both AND and XOR implementations on the same qubit — something impossible without this “flaw.” Only because AND implementation overflowed into one extra qubit, I could make 2 distinct measurements of the 2 gates acting on the same qubits.

Now, let’s dive deeper into a curious realization: if quantum states can’t be duplicated, how is it that electrons — a quantum particle — can simulate classical bits with ease? The answer lies in how electrons work in classical circuits. Instead of focusing on the quantum properties of each individual electron, classical computing only cares about the charge they collectively build up. Each wire doesn’t depend on the identity of the exact electrons flowing through it; it only measures the charge, which represents a binary state (0 or 1).

Let’s simplify with an analogy: imagine sending water through pipes. The classical system only cares about how much water reaches the end — not which exact water molecules made it there. In quantum systems, though, each individual water molecule’s unique properties would matter, making it an entirely different and more complex challenge.

This exercise taught me a profound lesson: the “bizarre” nature of quantum computing lies not just in its potential for revolution, but in the way it forces us to think differently about computation itself. By digging deep into these differences, we don’t just replicate classical systems — we learn to appreciate the distinct strengths and challenges of quantum technology.

If you didn’t grasp it all on the first read, go through it again — because understanding this difference between classical and quantum systems will give you an entirely new perspective on the future of computing.
